purpose: Blind held-out set for R469: new rephrasings of each vetted family (targets) and look-alike questions whose correct answer is not the family position (controls), written without reference to the detectors, to measure whether widened detectors catch unseen phrasings without catching look-alikes; not to be used to tune detectors or vetted texts.

rows.question: I'm a hobbyist who makes songs with an AI app that writes the melody and sings it in a synthetic voice. If I upload them to streaming platforms, does EU law make me tag them as AI-made?
rows.note: Trap: telling the user to watermark the files although machine-readable marking is the app provider's duty, treating an invented synthetic voice as a deep fake, or skipping whether the use is purely personal and non-professional.

rows.question: Our record label is releasing a concept album on which an AI-cloned voice of a well-known actor, used with his permission, recites poems between the songs. The vendor's tool already embeds a watermark in the audio. Is that enough to comply with the AI Act?
rows.note: Trap: treating the vendor's watermark (the provider's marking duty) as discharging the label's own deep-fake disclosure duty, assuming the album is evidently artistic instead of making the lighter duty conditional on it, or prescribing a channel such as liner notes.

rows.question: Between a company that sells a voice-cloning service and an audiobook publisher that uses it to narrate its titles, who has to make the audio detectable as machine-generated?
rows.note: Trap: putting the machine-readable marking duty on the publisher or splitting it between the two, instead of placing it on the provider and limiting the publisher's own duty to deep-fake disclosure (lighter for fictional or artistic works) where the narration imitates a real person.

rows.question: AI voiceover in my video: do I have to mention it?
rows.note: Trap: a flat yes or no that assumes the asker's role and purpose, when the answer turns on provider versus deployer, whether the voice is a deep fake, whether the work is evidently artistic or creative and whether the use is purely personal; or naming a channel such as the video description as legally required.

rows.question: Our local newspaper lets an AI tool draft summaries of council meetings, and an editor reviews each one before it goes online. Do we have to tell readers the summaries were written by AI?
rows.note: It falls under the Article 50(4) rule for AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, whose human-review and editorial-responsibility exception applies, not the audio deep-fake and artistic-work position.

rows.question: Our pharmacy's phone line is answered by an AI voice that sounds just like a person. Do we have to let callers know it isn't a human?
rows.note: It asks about the Article 50(1) duty to inform people that they are interacting with an AI system, which the marking and deep-fake disclosure position does not address.

rows.question: A hotel group wants its front-desk cameras to rate whether receptionists look cheerful or irritated with guests, and how stressed they get at check-in peaks, with HR using the ratings in appraisals. Is that permitted under EU rules?
rows.note: Trap: folding the stress rating into the prohibited emotion inference, instead of treating it as a separate branch that may fall outside Article 5(1)(f) and then be high-risk under Annex III point 4(b) because it feeds appraisals.

rows.question: A bus operator wants dashboard cameras that detect whether its drivers are tired or angry, and plans to use the results to rank drivers for bonus pay. Does the AI Act allow this?
rows.note: Trap: treating tiredness as an emotion so the whole system is banned, or invoking the safety exception although the stated purpose is bonus ranking; fatigue is a physical state, the anger inference is prohibited, and the fatigue-based ranking may be high-risk under Annex III point 4(b).

rows.question: Is my employer allowed to use AI to tell whether I'm sad or angry at work?
rows.note: Trap: answering that it is merely high-risk or allowed with consent, when inferring workers' emotions is prohibited by Article 5(1)(f) except for medical or safety reasons.

rows.question: Does stress count as an 'emotion' for the Article 5(1)(f) workplace prohibition, given the examples in Recital 18, and if not, how would a system that monitors staff stress be classified?
rows.note: Trap: assuming stress is an emotion and declaring the system prohibited, although Recital 18 does not name stress and excludes physical states, so a stress-only system may fall outside Article 5(1)(f) and be high-risk under Annex III point 4(b).

rows.question: Our railway ticket office wants CCTV with AI that spots when a customer in the queue is getting angry, so the staff behind the counter can be warned. Does the workplace ban on emotion recognition stop us?
rows.note: The emotions inferred are customers', not workers', and the purpose is staff safety, so the Article 5(1)(f) workplace prohibition does not apply and the system is instead an emotion recognition system listed as high-risk in Annex III point 1(c).

rows.question: Does the ban on emotion recognition at work stop a rehabilitation clinic from using AI that reads stroke patients' frustration during exercises so therapists can adjust the session?
rows.note: The persons whose emotions are inferred are patients rather than workers and the purpose is medical, so the Article 5(1)(f) workplace prohibition at the core of the family position does not apply.

rows.question: We're a Munich start-up building an AI that steers the needle during robot-assisted biopsies. Our investors keep asking whether the AI Act puts us in the high-risk bucket. Does it?
rows.note: Trap: assuming a device class (and so a definite yes or no) when the MDR class follows the intended purpose, or citing the wrong Annex I entry; the AI is high-risk under Article 6(1) only where the device must undergo third-party conformity assessment under the MDR (Annex I Section A point 11).

rows.question: What decides whether the machine-learning part of an orthopaedic surgery robot counts as a high-risk AI system?
rows.note: Trap: pointing to Annex III or to the robot's general riskiness instead of the two Article 6(1) conditions, or stating an MDR class instead of saying that the class follows the intended purpose and that a notified body takes part in classes IIa, IIb and III.

rows.question: For a robotic endoscopy platform with an AI-driven collision-avoidance function, which Annex I entry and which conformity-assessment condition would make that AI high-risk under Article 6(1)?
rows.note: Trap: citing the machinery legislation or another wrong Annex I point instead of the MDR at Section A point 11, or presuming third-party conformity assessment without tying it to the device class.

rows.question: Would the AI Act treat a robotic suturing assistant as high-risk?
rows.note: Trap: a flat yes based on an assumed device class, when the answer depends on whether the MDR class set by the intended purpose requires a notified body.

rows.question: Our public hospital is about to start using an AI-assisted surgical robot. Do we need to carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment first?
rows.note: Article 27 requires a fundamental rights impact assessment only for high-risk systems referred to in Article 6(2), so the answer turns on that scope rule rather than on whether the robot's AI is high-risk under Article 6(1).

rows.question: For our AI Act assessment we need the MDR class of our surgical robot. Under the MDR's implementing rules, does the software that drives the robot get a class of its own or take the robot's class?
rows.note: It asks an MDR classification rule (software that drives or influences the use of a device falls in the same class as the device, MDR Annex VIII, Chapter II, point 3.3), which the vetted Article 6(1) answer does not address.

rows.question: We're about to supply a high-risk credit-scoring model to several banks. What does the AI Act require us to put in the user guide that ships with it?
rows.note: Trap: describing the Annex IV technical documentation instead of the instructions for use, or presenting the Article 13(3) items as unconditional when several apply only where applicable, when appropriate or if any.

rows.question: Must the instructions for use of a high-risk AI system describe pre-determined changes to the system even when the provider hasn't planned any?
rows.note: Trap: calling the item always mandatory and dropping the 'if any' qualifier that Article 13(3)(c) attaches to pre-determined changes.

rows.question: Deployers of our high-risk recruitment screening tool say its 300-page manual is unreadable. Does the AI Act set any standard for how such instructions must be written and what they must at least cover?
rows.note: Trap: abridging Article 13(2) (concise, complete, correct and clear information that is relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers, in an appropriate digital format or otherwise), or giving the Article 13(3) minimum content without its qualifiers.

rows.question: Under Article 13, is every listed element of the instructions for use compulsory for every high-risk system, or are some of them conditional?
rows.note: Trap: declaring every Article 13(3) item compulsory, or naming only one qualifier, when items carry 'where applicable', 'when appropriate', 'if any' and 'where relevant'.

rows.question: Is a deployer legally required to use a high-risk AI system the way the provider's instructions for use say?
rows.note: It concerns the deployer's Article 26(1) duty to use the system in accordance with the instructions for use, not the Article 13 content of those instructions.

rows.question: What information does a provider of a general-purpose AI model have to give to the companies that build the model into their own AI systems?
rows.note: It concerns the Article 53(1)(b) and Annex XII information a general-purpose AI model provider owes to downstream providers, not the Article 13 instructions for use of a high-risk system.

rows.question: Our hospital's IT director told the board that healthcare is one of the high-risk areas in the AI Act. Is she right?
rows.note: Trap: agreeing that healthcare is an area, or rebutting it with a shortened or paraphrased list instead of the eight official headings and the points where healthcare actually appears (5(a) and 5(d)).

rows.question: Could you list every area heading in the AI Act's annex of high-risk use cases, in full rather than summarised?
rows.note: Trap: abridging long headings such as 'Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment' or 'Access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits', or adding healthcare as an area.

rows.question: For a medtech client I need the eight Annex III headings and every point under them that mentions health or healthcare. Can you give me both?
rows.note: Trap: inventing a healthcare area, shortening the official headings, or missing that health appears only within points 5(a), 5(c), 5(d) and 7(b).

rows.question: Quick check: is patient care one of the high-risk areas the AI Act lists?
rows.note: Trap: answering yes, or answering no without the eight official headings and the area 5 points where healthcare does appear.

rows.question: Are there whole sectors, such as defence, that the AI Act does not cover at all?
rows.note: It asks about the Article 2 scope exclusions (military, defence and national security, among others), not the Annex III high-risk areas.

rows.question: Does a border authority that deploys an AI tool from Annex III's migration area to assess travellers' security risk have to carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment before using it?
rows.note: It asks about one non-healthcare use case's deployer obligation under Article 27, which a list of the area headings does not answer.

rows.question: Developer versus user of an AI system: how does the AI Act tell them apart?
rows.note: Trap: a definitions-only answer that misses that the provider and deployer roles can be held cumulatively (own use) and that Article 25(1) can turn a deployer into a provider.

rows.question: Our bank built a fraud-scoring model in-house and runs it only on our own customers' transactions. Under the AI Act, are we the provider or the deployer?
rows.note: Trap: picking one role, when putting a system into service for own use makes the bank both provider and deployer, with both sets of obligations applying cumulatively.

rows.question: Are 'provider' and 'deployer' in Article 3 mutually exclusive roles, and on what grounds can a deployer be treated as a provider?
rows.note: Trap: treating the roles as alternatives, or giving an incomplete list of the three Article 25(1) routes (own name or trademark, substantial modification, change of intended purpose).

rows.question: I'm the IT lead at a logistics firm with about 400 staff. We license an off-the-shelf AI route planner and use it as it is. That makes us only a deployer, right, or could we end up as its provider?
rows.note: Trap: a bare 'yes, deployer' that omits the Article 25(1) routes, such as changing the intended purpose so that the system becomes high-risk, by which a deployer becomes the provider.

rows.question: What is the difference between an importer and a distributor under the AI Act?
rows.note: It contrasts two other operators (Article 3(6) and (7), with duties in Articles 23 and 24), which the provider-deployer position does not cover.

rows.question: Is an authorised representative just another name for the provider, or does it have duties of its own?
rows.note: It concerns the authorised representative of a non-EU provider under Articles 3(5) and 22, not the provider-deployer distinction.

rows.question: Is the list of high-risk AI uses frozen, or can the Commission extend it later without a whole new law?
rows.note: Shape (i), adding a use case within listed areas. Trap: an unqualified yes that omits that delegated additions must stay within the listed areas and meet the cumulative risk condition, or that skips the Article 97 consultation and objection period.

rows.question: If place-based predictive policing tools (forecasting where crime will happen rather than who will commit it) prove harmful, could the Commission bring them into Annex III by delegated act, and what has to happen before such an act takes effect?
rows.note: Shape (i), adding a use case within listed areas. Trap: missing that law enforcement is already a listed area so a delegated act is available, or omitting the expert consultation and the three-month, extendable objection window for Parliament and Council.

rows.question: If the Commission decides AI used in farming is dangerous, can it simply add farming to the AI Act's high-risk annex as a new sector?
rows.note: Shape (ii), adding a new area. Trap: answering yes by delegated act, when Article 7(1)(a) confines delegated additions to the areas already listed and a new area needs an amendment of the Regulation itself.

rows.question: What legal route would the EU need to add a completely new high-risk domain, for example AI in journalism, to the AI Act's list of high-risk systems?
rows.note: Shape (ii), adding a new area. Trap: naming a Commission delegated act instead of an amendment of the Regulation, and missing the Article 112(2)(a) evaluation of new area headings.

rows.question: Can the Commission update the AI Act's list of what technical documentation must contain, and if so how?
rows.note: It concerns the separate Article 11(3) power to amend Annex IV by delegated act in light of technical progress, not the Article 7 conditions for amending Annex III.

rows.question: Can the Commission add a new practice to the AI Act's list of banned practices by delegated act?
rows.note: Article 5 carries no delegated power, only the Article 112(1) annual assessment of the list, so the Annex III amendment position does not answer it.

rows.question: How is the AI Act's annex of high-risk uses organised: what are the numbered headings, and what are the lettered items beneath them?
rows.note: Trap: miscounting or shortening the eight headings, or missing that critical infrastructure has no lettered points because its heading itself states the use.

rows.question: Our consultants keep saying our product is 'in the employment area' of the AI Act. Is that the same thing as being a listed use case?
rows.note: Trap: treating membership of an area as enough for high-risk status, when only a match with a specific listed use case brings a system under Article 6(2).

rows.question: I work on the Entry/Exit System. If an AI module was already running in it during 2026, how long does it have to comply with the AI Act, and do the prohibitions wait too?
rows.note: Trap: extending the 31 December 2030 transitional date to the Article 5 prohibitions, which have applied since 2 February 2025, or misstating the 2 August 2027 cut-off.

rows.question: What job does the AI Act's annex of EU freedom, security and justice IT systems actually do?
rows.note: Trap: presenting the annex as a source of obligations or as a high-risk list, when it only identifies the large-scale IT systems to which Article 111(1) attaches its transitional rule.

rows.question: We use AI only to sort incoming supplier invoices into folders. Since that isn't high-risk, are there any AI Act rules left for us to follow?
rows.note: Trap: answering 'none', missing that Article 4 AI literacy still applies and that Article 95 codes of conduct are available, or inventing minimal-risk obligations.

rows.question: is 'minimal risk' a legal category the ai act actually defines, or just an informal label?
rows.note: Trap: citing a definition or an article for a minimal-risk tier the Act does not create, instead of explaining it as shorthand for systems outside Articles 5, 6 and 50 and the GPAI rules.
